questions.stem: According to accretion theory, how did the Earth form?
options: Dust and rock around the young Sun collided and stuck, growing into larger bodies
A large blob of molten rock was thrown out of the Sun and cooled into a solid sphere
Gas in the solar nebula cooled directly into one solid planet in a single event
A passing star pulled material from the Sun, which then condensed into planets
questions.explanation: Accretion theory holds that grains in the disc around the young Sun collided and stuck, forming planetesimals that grew by further collisions and gravitational attraction into protoplanets and planets. The Earth was not ejected from the Sun or formed in one step.

questions.stem: As accreting bodies grew larger, why did gravity become more important than chemical sticking in collecting material?
options: Gravity increases with mass, so larger bodies pulled in more material
Larger bodies were colder, so their surfaces became stickier to incoming dust
Gravity only acts once a body has formed a liquid iron core at its centre
Larger bodies spun faster, which drew in material from the surrounding nebula
questions.explanation: Small grains stick by electrostatic and chemical forces, but the gravitational pull of a body grows with its mass. Once planetesimals reached kilometre sizes, gravity dominated and they swept up material around them. Gravity acts between all masses, not only bodies with cores.

questions.stem: What is meant by the 'potato radius' of a celestial body?
options: The radius above which a body begins to orbit a planet rather than the Sun
The radius above which a body's gravity pulls it into a near-sphere
The radius below which a body's gravity is too weak to hold an atmosphere
The radius at which a body's core becomes hot enough to melt its iron
questions.explanation: Below the potato radius a body's material strength resists its weak gravity, so it keeps an irregular, potato-like shape. Above it, gravity overcomes the strength of the material and pulls the body into a near-sphere. It is about shape, not atmospheres or melting.

questions.stem: The potato radius was estimated at about 200 km for icy bodies and about 300 km for rocky bodies. Why is it smaller for icy bodies?
options: Icy bodies orbit further from the Sun, where gravity is much stronger
Ice is weaker than rock, so less gravity is needed to deform it into a sphere
Ice is denser than rock, so icy bodies have stronger gravity at the same size
Ice melts as an icy body forms, so all icy bodies begin as liquid spheres
questions.explanation: The radius at which a body rounds depends on how strong its material is compared with its gravity. Ice yields more easily than rock, so icy bodies become round at a smaller size. Ice is less dense than rock, not more, which would work the other way.

questions.stem: Mars's moon Phobos has a mean radius of about 11 km and an irregular shape. Which explanation is consistent with the potato radius concept?
options: It was spherical when it formed but has since been melted into shape by the Sun
Its rock is too weak to resist gravity, so it has been pulled out of shape
It orbits a planet, and only bodies orbiting the Sun can become spherical
Its gravity is too weak to overcome the strength of its rock
questions.explanation: A body as small as Phobos is far below the roughly 300 km potato radius for rock, so its gravity cannot deform its rock into a sphere. Large moons such as our own Moon are round, so orbiting a planet does not prevent a spherical shape.

questions.stem: A student plots shape against mean radius for many asteroids and moons. Bodies under 150 km are all irregular, bodies over 400 km are all round, and between them both shapes occur. What is the best conclusion?
options: Shape depends only on composition, because the round bodies are the icy ones
Rounding happens over a transition range set by composition as well as size
Size has no clear link to shape, because some mid-sized bodies are irregular
All bodies over 150 km are round, and the irregular ones were measured wrongly
questions.explanation: The data show a clear size trend with a transition zone where material strength, which differs between ice and rock, decides the outcome. This matches estimates of about 200 km for icy and 300 km for rocky bodies. The overlap does not remove the size trend or justify discarding data.

questions.stem: What is planetary differentiation?
options: The gradual cooling of a planet's surface after it has formed
The loss of a planet's light gases to space during accretion
The separation of a planet's materials into layers by density
The splitting of a planet's crust into separate moving plates
questions.explanation: In differentiation, a planet that is hot enough for its materials to move separates them by density: dense iron and nickel sink to form a core, while lighter silicates form the mantle and crust. Plate formation came later and is a different process.

questions.stem: Which conditions in the early Earth allowed differentiation to occur?
options: Heat from impacts, radioactive decay and compression melted much of the planet
Cold temperatures froze the outer layers, which squeezed iron towards the centre
Strong winds in the early atmosphere sorted surface rocks by their weight
Ocean water dissolved light minerals and carried them up to the surface
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy from impacts, the decay of radioactive isotopes and gravitational compression heated the young Earth so much of it melted. In molten or softened material, dense iron could sink and lighter silicates could rise. Cooling would have slowed, not driven, separation.

questions.stem: In a model of differentiation, a student shakes iron filings, sand and small polystyrene beads in a jar of golden syrup and leaves it to settle. What does the syrup represent?
options: The hot, partly molten early Earth in which materials could move
The liquid outer core that surrounds the solid inner core today
The early oceans that formed when water vapour condensed
The early atmosphere that was released by volcanic outgassing
questions.explanation: The syrup is a viscous medium that lets the solid particles move and separate by density, as materials did in the hot, partly molten young Earth. The filings sink like iron forming the core, while light beads rise like crustal material.

questions.stem: Which is the most important limitation of the golden syrup model of planetary differentiation?
options: It cannot be repeated, because the same materials will settle in a different order each time
It shows density separation, but not a planet's pressure, heat or timescale
It uses solid particles, so it cannot show any separation of materials by their densities
It shows dense materials rising to the surface, the reverse of what happened in Earth
questions.explanation: The model does show density separation, which is its purpose, but it happens under room conditions in minutes, in gravity pointing one way down a jar rather than towards a centre. It cannot represent the pressure, temperature, melting and timescale of the real process.

questions.stem: Why did iron and nickel, rather than silicate minerals, end up concentrated in the Earth's core?
options: They are lighter, so they were pushed inwards as heavier minerals settled
They are much denser, so they sank through the softened interior under gravity
They have lower melting points, so they were the last materials to solidify
They are magnetic, so the Earth's magnetic field pulled them towards the centre
questions.explanation: Iron and nickel are far denser than silicate minerals, so in a hot, partly molten Earth they sank towards the centre under gravity. The magnetic field is generated by the liquid outer core after it formed; it did not cause the separation.

questions.stem: How did the first solid crust of the geosphere form?
options: Iron rose from the core and cooled at the surface into rock
The surface of a molten Earth cooled and solidified into rock
Sediment from early rivers was compacted into layers of rock
Meteorites piled up on the surface and fused into a solid shell
questions.explanation: The early Earth had a molten surface, often described as a magma ocean. As it lost heat to space, the outer layer cooled and crystallised into the first crust. Sediment needs existing rock, water and weathering, so sedimentary rock came later.

questions.stem: Earth's earliest atmosphere was rich in hydrogen and helium, but little of these gases remains. What is the main reason?
options: They were absorbed by the iron core during differentiation and are trapped there
These light gases escaped Earth's gravity or were stripped by the solar wind
They reacted with oxygen produced by early plants and were converted into water vapour
They dissolved into the first oceans and were then locked away in sedimentary rocks
questions.explanation: Hydrogen and helium molecules are light and fast-moving, so a young, hot Earth could not hold them, and the solar wind helped strip them away. Photosynthesis evolved far later, so it cannot explain their loss.

questions.stem: Which process mainly produced Earth's secondary atmosphere?
options: Photosynthesis by early land plants releasing large amounts of oxygen
Evaporation of the first oceans, releasing hydrogen and helium gases
Weathering of crustal rocks, releasing oxygen from silicate minerals
Volcanic outgassing of water vapour, carbon dioxide and nitrogen
questions.explanation: Gases trapped in the interior were released through volcanoes, building an atmosphere of mostly water vapour, carbon dioxide and nitrogen with little free oxygen. Oxygen built up much later, from photosynthesis by microbes rather than land plants.

questions.stem: Two sources are proposed for the water that formed Earth's hydrosphere. Which pair is supported by evidence?
options: Rain from the solar nebula, and water squeezed out of rocks by plate collisions
Outgassing from the interior, plus delivery by comets and water-rich meteorites
Melting of an early ice cap, and release of water by photosynthesis in the early oceans
Condensation of hydrogen from the Sun, and chemical reactions in the iron core
questions.explanation: Water vapour released by volcanic outgassing condensed as the surface cooled, and comets and water-rich meteorites such as carbonaceous chondrites are thought to have added more. Photosynthesis uses water, so it cannot have created the oceans.

questions.stem: What had to happen before water vapour in the early atmosphere could form oceans?
options: The crust had to break into plates to form ocean basins
The Moon had to form to raise tides on the early surface
The surface had to cool below the boiling point of water
The atmosphere had to gain free oxygen from photosynthesis
questions.explanation: While the surface was hotter than water's boiling point, water stayed as vapour. Once it cooled, the vapour condensed and fell as rain, collecting in low areas. Oxygen in the atmosphere came much later, so it was not needed for oceans.

questions.stem: Which property of S waves allowed seismologists to conclude that the outer core is liquid?
options: S waves speed up when they enter liquids
S waves cannot travel through liquids
S waves travel faster than P waves
S waves only travel along the surface
questions.explanation: S waves are shear waves, and liquids cannot support shear, so S waves stop at a liquid layer. No direct S waves arrive across a large area on the far side of the Earth from an earthquake, showing that the outer core is liquid. P waves, not S waves, are the faster body waves.

questions.stem: Seismic waves follow curved paths through the mantle rather than straight lines. Why?
options: They are deflected by Earth's magnetic field, so they travel in curved paths
Their speed increases with depth, so they refract gradually back towards the surface
Their speed decreases with depth, so they are reflected straight back from the core
They are pulled downwards by gravity, so they bend towards the centre of the Earth
questions.explanation: As depth increases, pressure makes mantle rock more rigid, so seismic waves travel faster and are continuously refracted, curving back up towards the surface. Gravity and the magnetic field do not bend seismic waves.

questions.stem: When P waves pass from the mantle into the liquid outer core, they slow down sharply. What effect does this have?
options: They speed up and spread out, so P waves arrive everywhere on the far side
They turn into S waves, which then travel through the liquid outer core
They refract at the boundary, leaving a shadow zone with no direct P waves
They stop completely, so no P waves at all reach the far side of the Earth
questions.explanation: The sudden drop in speed bends P waves sharply at the core-mantle boundary, so a band at the surface receives no direct P waves: the P-wave shadow zone. P waves do pass through liquid, so some reach the far side, unlike S waves.

questions.stem: Inge Lehmann published her proposal of a solid inner core in 1936. Which observation did she explain?
options: No seismic waves at all arriving on the far side of the Earth
Faint P waves arriving inside the P-wave shadow zone
S waves passing straight through the centre of the Earth
Surface waves arriving before P waves at distant stations
questions.explanation: Under a model with a single liquid core, no P waves should reach the shadow zone, yet faint P waves were recorded there. Lehmann explained them as P waves reflected off a boundary inside the core, where an inner core with faster wave speeds begins.

questions.stem: Lehmann reasoned that some P waves were reflected off a boundary inside the core. What did this boundary tell her about the core's structure?
options: The core is hollow, so waves reflect off the inner surface of a liquid shell
Properties change inside the core, so an inner core differs from the outer core
The core is made of the same liquid throughout, with waves reflecting off its centre
The mantle extends deep into the core, so waves reflect off rock within the liquid
questions.explanation: Seismic waves reflect and refract only where wave speed changes, which happens at a boundary between materials with different properties. Lehmann's reflections required a second boundary inside the core, defining an inner core where P waves travel faster. A uniform core would give no such reflections.

questions.stem: In a practical model of seismic waves, a student shines a laser through layers of water and glass blocks. What is the strength of this model?
options: It shows waves changing direction at boundaries between different materials
It shows the actual speeds of P and S waves through the mantle and the core
It shows waves passing through solids but stopping at liquid layers, like S waves
It shows how seismic waves are produced by the movement of rock along faults
questions.explanation: Light refracts and reflects at boundaries where its speed changes, just as seismic waves do at boundaries inside the Earth. The model does not reproduce seismic speeds, and light passes through water, so it cannot show S waves stopping in liquid.

questions.stem: Seismographs at stations up to about 103 degrees from an earthquake record both P and S waves, while stations beyond that record no direct S waves. Which inference is valid?
options: A deep layer will not transmit shear waves, so part of the core is liquid
The Earth's interior is solid throughout, because P waves are recorded at the far stations
S waves travel too slowly to reach distant stations before they lose all of their energy
The far stations are on the ocean floor, where seismographs cannot detect any S waves
questions.explanation: The large S-wave shadow on the far side shows that S waves are blocked by a layer that cannot transmit shear, which is a liquid. Recording P waves does not show the interior is solid, because P waves also travel through liquids.

questions.stem: What does the lithosphere consist of?
options: The liquid outer core and the solid inner core
The crust and the rigid uppermost part of the mantle
The crust only, both oceanic and continental
The upper mantle and the asthenosphere below it
questions.explanation: The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell of the Earth, made of the crust together with the uppermost mantle, and it is broken into tectonic plates. The crust alone is only its top part.

questions.stem: Which description best fits the asthenosphere?
options: A hot, weak layer of the upper mantle that flows slowly like a stiff fluid
A cold, rigid layer of crust and mantle that is broken into the tectonic plates
A layer of liquid iron and nickel whose movement generates the magnetic field
A thin layer of solid rock at the surface that forms the continents and ocean floors
questions.explanation: The asthenosphere lies below the lithosphere. Its rock is close to its melting point and may be slightly partially molten, so it is weak and flows very slowly, allowing the rigid plates above to move. The rigid, broken shell is the lithosphere.

questions.stem: Which layer of the Earth is thinnest?
options: The lithosphere
The outer core
The mantle
The crust
questions.explanation: The crust is only about 5 to 10 km thick under the oceans and on average about 35 km under the continents, much thinner than any other layer. The lithosphere includes the crust plus uppermost mantle, so it must be thicker than the crust.

questions.stem: How does continental crust compare with oceanic crust?
options: It is thicker and less dense, and is made mostly of granitic rock
It is thinner and denser, and is made mostly of basaltic rock
It is thicker and denser, and is made mostly of basaltic rock
It is thinner and less dense, and is made mostly of granitic rock
questions.explanation: Continental crust is mostly granitic, with a density of about 2.7 g/cm³, and is much thicker than oceanic crust. Oceanic crust is basaltic, about 3.0 g/cm³, and thin. The lower density of continental crust is why it is not easily subducted.

questions.stem: The inner core is hotter than the outer core, yet the inner core is solid and the outer core is liquid. What explains this?
options: The magnetic field around the inner core holds its atoms in fixed positions as a solid crystal
Greater pressure at the centre raises iron's melting point above its temperature
The inner core is made of rock, while the outer core is made of a liquid iron and nickel mixture
The inner core loses heat to the outer core quickly, so it is actually cooler than the outer core
questions.explanation: Both layers are mostly iron and nickel, and temperature rises towards the centre. But the pressure there is so great that it raises the melting point of iron above the actual temperature, so the inner core stays solid. The inner core is not cooler or rocky.

questions.stem: How do temperature and pressure change from the crust to the centre of the Earth?
options: Temperature increases, but pressure decreases
Pressure increases, but temperature decreases
Both increase with depth
Both decrease with depth
questions.explanation: The weight of overlying rock makes pressure rise steadily with depth, and temperature also rises because of heat left from the Earth's formation and from radioactive decay. This combination explains why some deep layers are solid and others liquid.

questions.stem: Which layer is responsible for generating the Earth's magnetic field?
options: The inner core, where solid iron is permanently magnetised
The asthenosphere, where molten rock flows below the plates
The crust, where magnetic minerals are concentrated in ores
The outer core, where liquid iron flows and moves electric charge
questions.explanation: Convection of electrically conducting liquid iron in the outer core produces electric currents, which generate the magnetic field. The inner core is far too hot to stay permanently magnetised, as iron loses its magnetism above a certain temperature.

questions.stem: A sample of basalt has a mass of 90 g and displaces 30 mL of water. What is its density?
options: 2700 g/cm³
60 g/cm³
3.0 g/cm³
0.33 g/cm³
questions.explanation: Density = mass / volume = 90 g / 30 cm³ = 3.0 g/cm³, since 1 mL is 1 cm³. This matches typical oceanic crust. Dividing volume by mass gives 0.33, and subtracting gives 60, which are both slips.

questions.stem: A student measures four samples: granite 2.7, basalt 3.0, peridotite 3.3 and iron 7.9 g/cm³. Which layer does each sample represent, in this order?
options: Oceanic crust, continental crust, mantle, core
Continental crust, mantle, oceanic crust, core
Mantle, oceanic crust, continental crust, core
Continental crust, oceanic crust, mantle, core
questions.explanation: Granite represents continental crust, basalt oceanic crust, and peridotite, an olivine-rich rock, the upper mantle. Iron represents the core. The densities rise in the same order as the layers do with depth.

questions.stem: The Earth's average density is about 5.5 g/cm³, but surface rocks have densities of only about 2.7 to 3.0 g/cm³. What does this show?
options: The surface rocks must have been measured with a systematic error
The oceans must make up a large share of the Earth's total mass
The interior must contain material much denser than surface rock
The interior must be hollow or contain large pockets of gas
questions.explanation: If surface rock is about 3 g/cm³ but the whole planet averages about 5.5 g/cm³, the material deeper down must be much denser, which is consistent with an iron-rich core. A hollow interior would lower the average, not raise it.

questions.stem: Pure iron at the surface has a density of about 7.9 g/cm³, but the core's density is estimated at about 10 to 13 g/cm³. What is the best explanation?
options: Heat in the core expands its atoms, which increases the density of iron
The core contains large amounts of water trapped under very high pressure
Enormous pressure at depth compresses the core's iron into a smaller volume
The core is made of rock that is naturally denser than any form of iron
questions.explanation: Pressure at the core is millions of times atmospheric pressure, which squeezes iron atoms closer together and raises its density above the surface value. Heating would expand iron and lower its density, which is the opposite effect.

questions.stem: Iron meteorites are made mostly of iron and nickel. What are they thought to be?
options: Fragments of the cores of differentiated asteroids that were broken apart
Pieces of the Earth's own core thrown into space by volcanic eruptions
Lumps of metal that condensed directly from the Sun's outer atmosphere
Fragments of the crusts of rocky planets that were melted by impacts
questions.explanation: Iron meteorites come from the metallic cores of asteroids that melted and differentiated and were later shattered by collisions. They give a sample of planetary core material, supporting an iron-nickel composition for the Earth's core. No eruption could launch core material into space.

questions.stem: Chondrites are stony meteorites that were never melted. Why are they useful evidence for the Earth's overall composition?
options: They formed in the Earth's mantle, so they show the composition of the asthenosphere
They preserve the original mix of material from which planets like the Earth accreted
They are pieces of the Earth's crust, so they match the composition of surface rocks
They are made of pure iron, so they show what the inner core is made of
questions.explanation: Because chondrites never melted or separated into layers, they keep the bulk composition of early solar system material. Comparing them with crustal rocks shows the Earth's surface is short of iron, implying the missing iron is concentrated in the core.

questions.stem: Stony-iron meteorites called pallasites contain crystals of the silicate mineral olivine set in iron-nickel metal. Which part of a differentiated body are they thought to represent?
options: The material that never separated into any layers
The boundary between a metal core and a silicate mantle
The outer crust formed as a magma ocean cooled
The mixture of gases released by early outgassing
questions.explanation: Pallasites combine mantle-type silicate crystals and core-type metal, so they are thought to come from near the core-mantle boundary of a differentiated asteroid. Undifferentiated material is represented by chondrites, which have not separated into metal and silicate.

questions.stem: Why do scientists use meteorite densities as well as their compositions when building models of the Earth's interior?
options: Meteorites become denser in space, which shows how pressure affects rocks
Iron meteorites are about as dense as iron, which supports a dense metallic core
Meteorites are all lighter than surface rocks, which supports a hollow core
Meteorites have the same density as the asthenosphere, which shows it is liquid
questions.explanation: Iron meteorites are much denser than stony meteorites and crustal rocks, matching the high density needed in the core to give the Earth its average of about 5.5 g/cm³. Together with seismic data, this supports an iron-nickel core.
